questions.q: Which of the following elements is classified as a metalloid? (a) Copper (b) Silicon (c) Sulfur (d) Oxygen
questions.a: The correct answer is (b) Silicon. Silicon is a classic metalloid used extensively in computer chips because its electrical conductivity is intermediate between metals and non-metals. A student who chooses (a) copper confuses metalloids with pure metals, which are excellent conductors and malleable. Choosing (c) or (d) shows confusion with non-metals, which are typically poor conductors and lack metallic luster.

questions.q: Why is silicon described as a "metalloid" rather than a true metal, even though it has a shiny, metallic appearance?
questions.a: Silicon has a shiny luster like a metal, but it is extremely brittle and shatters when struck instead of being malleable or ductile. Furthermore, its ability to conduct electricity is much lower than that of metals. A student who thinks silicon is a true metal fails to distinguish between surface appearance (luster) and bulk mechanical properties like brittleness and electrical behavior.

questions.q: A science student tests an unknown grey solid found in the laboratory. It looks shiny like a piece of iron, but when struck with a hammer, it instantly crumbles into a fine powder instead of flattening into a sheet. What does this behavior tell us about the classification of this substance?
questions.a:
The working steps are: 
1. Observe the physical appearance: shiny (suggests metallic luster). 
2. Observe the mechanical response to force: crumbles into powder (shows extreme brittleness, which is a non-metallic property). 
3. Conclude that the substance has mixed characteristics. 
4. Classify it as a metalloid. 
A student who concludes it is a metal is focusing only on the shiny appearance and ignoring the brittle nature characteristic of metalloids and some non-metals.

questions.q: Compare the electrical conductivity of a copper wire, a sulfur lump, and a silicon chip at room temperature. How do their conductivity levels reflect their classification?
questions.a: Copper is a metal and has very high electrical conductivity, allowing free electrons to move easily. Sulfur is a non-metal and is an insulator, showing virtually no electrical conductivity. Silicon is a metalloid with intermediate conductivity—higher than sulfur but lower than copper—making it a semiconductor. A student who states that silicon conducts electricity as well as copper does not understand the intermediate nature of metalloid electronic properties.

questions.q: An engineer wants to build a device that needs a material with high malleability to be drawn into thin wires for high-current household wiring. She considers using a metalloid like arsenic or silicon. Is this a sound engineering choice, and why or why not?
questions.a: This is NOT a sound choice. Metalloids like silicon and arsenic are brittle and lack malleability and ductility; they cannot be drawn into wires. Furthermore, their electrical conductivity is too low for efficient high-current power transmission compared to metals like copper or aluminium. A student who approves this choice misunderstands the mechanical and electrical limitations of metalloids.

questions.q: Design a simple home investigation to distinguish between a metal rod, a lump of sulfur, and a silicon piece using everyday items like a battery, a small bulb, and a hammer.
questions.a:
A good design involves two tests: 
1. Mechanical Test: Gently tap each material with a hammer to check for malleability versus brittleness. 
2. Electrical Test: Connect each material in a simple electric circuit with a battery and bulb to see if the bulb lights up. 
A poor answer would suggest melting them or tasting them, which are unsafe and fail to test conductivity or brittleness.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Metalloids are a special group of elements that possess properties ______ between those of metals and non-metals.

Fill in the blank: When you look at a solar panel on a rooftop or inside a computer processor powering a ______, you are seeing materials that do not quite fit the strict definitions of metals or non-metals.
What is Metalloids? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Metalloids are a special group of elements that possess properties intermediate between those of metals and non-metals.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Metalloids?
questions.a: Students frequently assume that any element with a shiny, lustrous appearance must be a metal and therefore a good conductor of electricity and heat in all conditions.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Can classify an element as a metal, non-metal, or metalloid based on physical properties such as luster, malleability, brittleness, and electrical conductivity.
